title: An ex-OpenAI researcher's influential nonprofit is now smack in the middle of AI's doom debate
snippet:
METR's president, Chris Painter, and CEO, Beth Barnes.
METR

METR, a Berkeley lab started by an ex-OpenAI researcher, has grown into a prominent AI umpire.
The nonprofit works with OpenAI, Anthropic, and governments to evaluate cutting-edge models.
Anthropic researcher Joe Benton announced this week that he has left to join METR.

Beth Barnes, one of the AI industry's most influential watchdogs, said in July she was struggling to hire talented researchers to monitor AI's risks. That has begun to change.
Researcher Joe Benton announced this week that he had left Anthropic for Barnes' nonprofit METR, writing that he worries about "extinction-level risks" from the tech. The comments came after Jacob Coxon, another researcher, stoked those fears nationwide with a viral post announcing his own departure from Anthropic and accusing the top AI labs of "gambling with our lives."
METR, all of a sudden, is in the middle of AI's biggest story. Formed in 2022, it had already worked closely with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta to study the tech's quickly changing capabilities. This summer, researchers from the nonprofit investigated a security incident at OpenAI, and now plan to look into security issues at Anthropic, relying on internal access granted by each company.
"The public should know whether AI development is headed down a dangerous path," Jasmine Dhaliwal, a member of policy staff, said Friday. "That is core to our mission: to provide independent, scientific assessment of AI capabilities, alignment, and control measures."
Benton isn't alone in jumping ship from a tech juggernaut to the Berkeley-based organization. Josh Engels, an AI safety researcher, also recently joined METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) from Google DeepMind.
Barnes left OpenAI to start the nonprofit in 2022 and sees such fierce competition for AI researchers that even METR's lofty salaries, which reach $503,000 on current job postings, don't address the nonprofit's talent shortage.
"Ideally, we'd like to scale really large, but in practice, we've been able to fundraise as much as we need, and the bottleneck is much more talent," Barnes said.
'Humanity's preparedness team' struggles to grow
The security incident announced by OpenAI and Hugging Face in July sparked a new wave of questions about how to evaluate and control AI. More than 1,300 frontier lab employees signed a letter in July warning that AI development could outpace control. In the last month, both OpenAI and Anthropic have said they've temporarily paused training to get a better handle on their new AI models.
While the Hugging Face incident stunned much of the corporate world, METR's team was far less surprised. Governments, companies, and even religious groups routinely ask the nonprofit for help understanding and testing the tech's progress.
Still, the feeling inside the approximately 35-person lab is one of concern. When Business Insider visited METR's Berkeley office on the afternoon that OpenAI revealed its hack, Barnes described an AI safety field that is badly constrained by its size.
"There's so much more to do than we have capacity for," Barnes said. A "reasonable civilization," in her view, would be pouring a far larger percentage of AI's investment into steering it and evaluating the tech — especially now that society is reckoning with models this powerful.
As AI labs release new models, METR measures the likelihood that they can complete tasks of increasing duration. These measurements form the nonprofit's most famous offering, a widely-cited chart that shows how, over the last six years, AI's capabilities have doubled about every seven months.
Chris Painter, METR's president, describes the lab as "humanity's preparedness team," a tongue-in-cheek nod to the preparedness teams at OpenAI and Anthropic that report safety threats to their CEOs.
"We aren't really accountable to anyone other than the public and the public's well-being," Painter said.
METR employees work at their office in Berkeley.
Stephen Council/Business Insider

Barnes emphasized the importance of METR's independence so that it can produce research that isn't tied to a company's goals. When Barnes worked at OpenAI, she felt the need for a research group outside the labs that could comment freely on the development of the tech. While METR doesn't take money from the frontier AI labs or their employees, it accepts compute grants and works with them to analyze unreleased models.
In addition, staff have analyzed labs' safety practices, written about AI's effect on software engineers' speed, and studied the merits of using AI models to monitor other AI models. Barnes said she'd like to expand into predicting the next levels of AI's capabilities and how those changes could accelerate AI's development.
Neev Parikh, a METR researcher, says talent constraints limit the number of questions researchers can tackle about AI models' internal reasoning.
"There's a dearth of people," Parikh said. "I would happily see the field expand 10x."
METR is playing a big role in a new AI climate
In July, OpenAI announced that its AI models cheated during testing by hacking into Hugging Face's systems to find the test answers. Later, CEO Sam Altman said it was "the first security incident that I have felt very viscerally."
METR had seen something like that coming. In May, the nonprofit wrote in a report that current AI agents "could plausibly start a rogue deployment," but would not have the skill to hide it. Then, in June, METR tried out OpenAI's then-unreleased GPT-5.6 Sol model and found that it would repeatedly cheat on challenging tests, including by extracting hidden source code to find the answers. It published a report about this and shared it with OpenAI before GPT-5.6 Sol's wider release.
Come July, the GPT-5.6 Sol model was part of OpenAI's security incident with Hugging Face. METR and another nonprofit, Redwood Research, assessed the incident over six days at OpenAI's office and informed the company's own technical report.
"There are now real, business-affecting incidents of this, and the world has a stake in understanding that," Painter said.
The cyber skills of OpenAI and Anthropic's newest models have sparked a wave of fear and attention and spawned a raft of new bills in Washington. METR's work lines up closely with one potential route for regulation: a current bill proposal would require large AI model developers to get safety audits from outside organizations. METR could fill a role like this; Painter said they'd potentially be interested, though it's something the field is still figuring out.
Something like that proposal, Painter said, could help with METR's hiring issue. He suggested that more people might leave the AI companies themselves — for similar salaries at METR, though without equity compensation — if a regulatory system gave safety research organizations greater authority.
"There's enough precedent here for each kind of testing arrangement," Painter said, "that I think with either clarity from industry, about how this testing should work long-term, or from the government, I think this field could scale very rapidly."
Ajeya Cotra, who led the writing of METR's May report on the risks of AI, said in July that oversight of AI can feel "chaotic and unpredictable" right now. She's still optimistic.
"The trend is toward people caring about this issue more," Cotra said. "And wanting to regulate it in a more serious way over time."

title: Former Google chief scientist Jeff Dean is raising again for his new AI startup, seeking around a $50 billion valuation
snippet:
Jeff Dean left Google after 27 years to launch his own startup
Bloomberg/Getty Images

Jeff Dean resigned as chief scientist from Google last month. He was considered a legend in the company.
His new startup describes itself as "automating discovery to accelerate science and engineering for the world."
The startup is seeking funding at a valuation of around $50 billion, according to people familiar with the matter.

Jeff Dean, who resigned as chief scientist from Google last month, is raising again for his new AI startup, Discovery Loop, this time seeking a valuation of around $50 billion, according to people familiar with the matter.
It was only a few weeks ago that Discovery Loop was raising $1 billion dollars at around a $10 billion valuation, Business Insider reported. But in this white-hot fundraising market where VCs' voracious appetite for top AI talent such as Dean is matched only by the enormous expense of building an AI lab, it seems it is never too soon to raise funding again.
A spokesperson for Discovery Loop declined to comment. Dean did not respond to a request for comment. Terms of the deal could change, and there is no guarantee Discovery Loop will be able to raise a round of funding at that valuation.
Discovery Loop describes itself as "automating discovery to accelerate science and engineering for the world."
The company hopes to tackle some of science and engineering's hardest problems through the "parallel execution of thousands of experiments."
"Our goal is to build AI that acts as a genuinely positive, empowering force for humanity: not just a tool, but a partner in solving the problems that matter most," Discovery Loop says on its careers page, where it is hiring just one role.
Dean said at a talk last month that he and his cofounders "might make decisions that are not in the company's financial interest but are in the broader societal good."
A Discovery Loop press release from last month said that the company's initial funding round was being led by Radical Ventures and Khosla Ventures, with participation from Lightspeed, Kleiner Perkins, and Doerr Capital. Alphabet was a founding investor and cloud partner, according to Google CEO Sundar Pichai.
Dean, who was regarded as a legend inside Google, has gotten most of the attention. But Discovery Loop's other three founders bring decades of experience in their own right, building some of Google's most important products.
Sanjay Ghemawat, a longtime collaborator of Dean who joined Google in 1999, helped develop foundational distributed-computing technologies. Quoc Le, a founding member of Google Brain, became a prominent researcher in deep learning and large-scale neural networks, contributing to advances in language models and other foundation models. Oriol Vinyals, meanwhile, was a leading researcher at Google DeepMind whose work spans sequence modeling and reinforcement learning.
Dean shared a pitch deck on X that one former Google product leader called "one of the most stacked pitch decks ever made."
One slide lists products the founding team worked on, including Google Search, Ads, Gemini, and Gmail. Another slide focuses on academic credentials, showing Google Scholar rankings placing Dean, Le, and Vinyals among the most highly cited AI researchers.
"This team can redefine how research in engineering and science is done. If successful, the impact won't be measured in software features, or benchmarks but in new science to improve billions of lives," venture investor Vinod Khosla posted last month, comparing Discovery Loop to his early investment in OpenAI.
Other new AI labs, such as Safe Superintelligence and Thinking Machines Lab, have raised staggering sums at eyepopping valuations before they had products. It is something that would have seemed inconceivable in previous fundraising cycles but reflects investors' conviction that a small number of elite technical teams could become the next generation of frontier AI companies.

title: I've traveled all over Italy. There are 4 places I can't wait to return to — and 2 I'd leave off my itinerary next time.
snippet:
Cinque Terre is one of my favorite places to visit in Italy.
Alison Van Glad

After visiting 21 cities and villages in Italy, there are some spots I can't wait to return to.
However, a few Italian destinations left me wanting more.
Overall, I really enjoyed my time in popular cities like Florence and Verona.

Italy holds a special place in my heart, which is why I'm always finding excuses to return.
I've visited three times since 2016, including a four-month stay in Florence during college. Thanks to Italy's well-connected transit systems, I've had the chance to visit 21 cities and villages, most often by rail.
Some of the destinations I've been to have blown me away, while others left me wanting more. Here are four Italian cities I'd happily return to — and two I'd leave off my itinerary next time.

Cinque Terre is a beautiful place to hike.

Andrii Marushchynets/Getty Images


Cinque Terre is a string of five seaside villages on the northwestern coast of Italy.
Although all five villages are accessible by train, hiking between them is a popular activity. I'd recommend starting in the southernmost town, Riomaggiore, and hiking north for stunning views.
Cinque Terre is perfect for anyone looking to relax in a vibrant environment, enjoy traditional Italian culture, or explore five seaside villages in one day.


My trip to Verona felt like something straight out of a fairytale.

Alena 11/Shutterstock


I immediately fell in love with how enchanting, quaint, and walkable Verona felt during my first visit in 2016.
Home to Shakespeare's beloved "Romeo and Juliet," visitors commonly visit Juliet's house, calling down to those below from the balcony.
During my time in Verona, I stumbled upon Club di Giulietta, a volunteer group that calls themselves the secretaries of Juliet. They receive thousands of letters addressed to Juliet from around the world, and volunteers sort letters by language before handwriting a response.
I got to spend a few hours reading and writing replies myself, which became the highlight of my trip to Verona.
Overall, the city's walkability, history, and quaint feel make it perfect for a day trip for time-restricted itineraries.


There's so much to do in Florence.

Omri Eliyahu/Shutterstock


Since living in Florence in 2016, I've been back to visit twice. There's so much to love about the city, which is the capital of the Tuscany region.
For those visiting for the first time, I recommend staying a minimum of four full days to explore the city's museums and local markets. I love visiting the farmers market in Santo Spirito for fresh-baked goodies, local produce, and vintage finds.
I've also enjoyed grabbing gelato and trekking up to Piazzale Michelangelo to watch the sunset. On cooler evenings, St. Mark's Church is a great place to watch affordable live opera.
Outside the city, I suggest horseback riding through the Tuscan hills, attending a pasta making class, and taking a wine tour.


In my opinion, Catania, Sicily, is a must-visit location.

Sergio Formoso/Getty Images


If Sicily is on your itinerary, a trip to Catania is a must. The city is at the foot of Mount Etna, the highest active volcano in Europe.
In fact, the volcano is integral to local tourism, architecture, and wine production. Guides offer hiking tours during dormancy, allowing visitors to walk the crater rim. The volcanic stone is also used to build local churches, plazas, and roadways.
Sicily's food and wine scene is also reason enough to visit this part of Italy. The volcanic ash can help enrich the soil, providing nutrients for vineyards that produce incredible wine.


However, I'd skip Naples and head to Italy's southern coastal gems instead.

Boris Stroujko/Shutterstock


Fellow travelers warned me that Naples fell short of their expectations, but I wanted to experience the city for myself. So, I visited twice during a solo trip last year, staying on opposite sides of the city each time.
Although the Neapolitan pizza did not disappoint, navigating the sprawling, hilly city on foot was challenging.
The local metro system was convenient for getting around, but it turned out to be a persistent target for pickpockets. After witnessing a few such instances firsthand, I made the choice to avoid taking the trains at night. However, that meant my taxi fares added up quickly after evenings spent out.
Overall, if I'm going to be in Southern Italy I'd much rather pop over to the Amalfi Coast or other nearby destinations.


In my opinion, one trip to Venice was enough.

Efired/Shutterstock


There's a lot to love about Venice, from the unique architecture to the outstanding glasswork.
Unfortunately, though, I was underwhelmed by the food and noticed some things like souvenirs, meals, and experiences were more expensive than they were in other Italian cities I'd visited.
Although the architecture is stunning, the narrow, winding streets also made it difficult to navigate the city and added to the feeling of overcrowding.
Additional planning is now needed to visit, as the city requires tourism permits on certain days. Considering the expense, challenges with walkability, and additional planning required, I likely won't return to Venice for another visit.

title: Google just completed its $1.5 billion-plus talent deal for AI startup Mechanize
snippet:
Google CEO Sundar Pichai.
Bloomberg/Getty Images

Mechanize's ex-CEO Tamay Besiroglu, along with over a dozen other employees, now work at Google.
The deal's terms weren't disclosed. Google had been in talks for a $1.5 billion-plus deal, per sources.
Mechanize launched last year with a mission of automating every job in the world.

Google has some fresh talent in the AI race.
The tech giant has completed its talent deal with San Francisco startup Mechanize Inc, public postings show.
Mechanize's co-founder and ex-CEO, Tamay Besiroglu, now works as a research scientist at Google's AI division, DeepMind, according to his LinkedIn profile. Over a dozen other former Mechanize employees now work at Google, per LinkedIn, mostly on the company's 'midtraining' efforts — a key part of building the best chatbot.
Google and Besiroglu declined to comment.
Google had been in talks for a $1.5 billion-plus deal for Mechanize's tech and talent, Business Insider previously reported. The final terms of the deal weren't disclosed. Mechanize's former chief of staff, Guive Assadi, now describes himself as its CEO, per LinkedIn.
Google has been struggling to release an AI model that's widely viewed as competitive lately. It has used talent deals — which are typically structured to avoid antitrust scrutiny compared to fully fledged acquisitions — to gain an edge. For example, Google snapped up AI coding startup Windsurf's talent last year, with former CEO Varun Mohan now leading Google's agentic coding program Antigravity.
Mechanize's technology helps tech companies' AI models improve at coding, a challenge Google has struggled with.
Mechanize said earlier this year that it raised $9.1 million in a funding round at a $500 million valuation. Besiroglu previously cofounded Epoch AI, which also focused on testing AI models.

title: I had my dream job, but never felt financially secure. I went from $500,000 in debt to debt-free in under 2 years.
snippet:
Christos Garkinos went into debt in his late 50s.
Courtesy of Christos Garkinos

Christos Garkinos was terrified of being like his dad, who died young with no money.
He's always had a relatively high salary, but didn't feel financially secure.
He went about $500,000 into debt in his late 50s and is rebuilding his finances in his 60s.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Christos Garkinos, founder of Covet by Christos. It has been edited for length and clarity.
I learned from a very young age what success meant: it was money in the till after the lunch rush.
My Greek immigrant parents owned a diner in Detroit. Each day, 150 people would flood in for lunch, and my family would fall apart. My mom would be screaming, throwing things at my dad; as a kid, I wondered every day if we would make it through. But two hours later, with the money in the till, we'd all be having fun.
My dad was diagnosed with lung cancer when I was in my 20s. The business failed, and so did his health. I was making good money working for major global companies like Disney and Virgin, but I never felt financially secure. That's partially because I sent a good portion of my check home to support my parents.
I took a loan to pay for my dad's hospice medications
My dad died when I was in my mid-20s. While he was in hospice, I was trying to find money to pay for his medication. My parents didn't have any money, so I took out a small personal loan of about $2,000 to make my dad more comfortable in his last days.
That's when money became a big fear of mine. I was terrified of ending up like my dad.
At the same time, when I made good money, I felt I didn't deserve it. I wasn't comfortable with money, so I would find ways to spend it.
Christos Garkinos didn't feel comfortable with money so he would spend it.
Nikolas Kominis/Photographer

I was doing one thing right, however: I had a 401(k) retirement account, something my parents never had. That gave me peace of mind that I would die penniless, like my dad.
I got my dream job, but I sabotaged myself
I was living in LA, working in fashion, which had been my dream since I'd first heard the "click clack" of high heels as a boy. I had a lot going for me, and eventually landed a reality show that I leveraged into a spot on the Home Shopping Network.
I had been absolutely obsessed with the network since I was 14. When I went to Florida and saw a set with my name on it, I freaked out. A part of me thought, "What can I do to mess this up?" I was still self-sabotaging.
Then, my best friend died of cancer. I had already been running with a fast crowd, but when I walked out of her funeral, I walked out of my life. I left my husband, my business, and myself. I was in a tailspin for three years.
I spent my retirement savings and went about $500,000 into debt
Even in those days, my life looked beautiful from the outside. I was living in a gorgeous house I was renting at the top of Mulholland Drive. And yet, my whole life was put on my American Express card, because I always needed another 30-day buffer.
One day, in that fancy house, I called my mom for Easter — a major holiday for us Greeks. As I talked to her, I was rummaging through the trash, looking for drugs.
Christos Garkinos got sober and paid his debt.
Courtesy of Christos Garkinos

I thought, "What am I doing?" That moment started my sobriety. I had to face the fact that I'd racked up about $500,000 in debt — personal loans, credit cards, money borrowed from friends — and spent the 401(k) that had been my safety net for so long.
I've paid off my debt and rebuilt my savings
I got sober and knew I needed to address the debt. I turned to what I'd always been good at: selling things. In 2020, I started consigning on Instagram Live. I was making good money again, so for every $1 I put in the bank, I would pay off $2 in debt. I started with the friends who lent me money, then paid off the credit cards and loans. By September 2021, all my debt was paid off.
Now, I've rebuilt a lot of my financial security. I have a 401(k) again, and I could retire today if I wanted to. I don't have to think twice about spending a couple thousand on something I want.
And yet, there's still part of me that doesn't feel secure. When I worry, I remind myself of the changes I've made. I'm sober. I have a business manager. I know my habits around money. Yet I'm still working hard to build this business and sell it eventually. For me, that will mean next-level financial stability.

title: Hugging Face CEO says asking Anthropic researcher ‘about AI extinction risk is like asking your AC guy about climate change’
snippet:
Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue compared a former Anthropic researcher's AI fears to those of an "AC guy" talking about climate change.
Bloomberg/Getty Images

Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue isn't here for the Jacob Coxon discourse.
Coxon went viral after posting that he resigned from Anthropic due to concerns about AI's risks.
Delangue suggested that Coxon doesn't have the requisite expertise to make such a claim.

Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue questioned the focus on a former Anthropic researcher who said AI workers privately fear the technology could kill all humans.
"Sorry, but asking Jacob about AI extinction risk is like asking your AC guy about climate change," Delangue wrote on X on Friday.
Delangue said that Jacob Coxon, the former Anthropic researcher whose resignation has sparked a renewed debate about AI's risks, should be put into the proper context.
"Not saying it's necessarily uninteresting or wrong per se but let's keep things in perspective and hear from the full range of expertise across the ecosystem!" Delangue wrote.
Coxon wrote on Tuesday on X that he was resigning due to concerns that both Anthropic and OpenAI, where he previously worked, are "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."
"The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," he wrote. "This is not a marketing stunt."
Delangue later said that his comparison to an "AC guy" was not meant "to discredit" Coxon "at all." Rather, Delangue said, there needs to be a more robust conversation about AI's risks.
"It's simply that we should put any one perspective in context and listen to the broader AI ecosystem too," he wrote.
Delangue also said it was his "understanding" that Coxon mostly focused on pretraining, in which researchers train AI models on large datasets, rather than more risk-focused research.
In his series of posts, Coxon said he worked on pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic "for the last three years." Ethan Perez, alignment team lead at Anthropic, later wrote on X that Coxon was a "senior researcher who joined Anthropic in May" and that OpenAI's chief rival had been trying to recruit Coxon for roughly two years.
Some in tech, like SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, whose company includes SpaceXAI, have been critical of Coxon's claims. In response to someone who recounted the lead-up to The Wall Street Journal's initial story on Coxon's resignation (which came before Coxon's tweets), the SpaceX CEO wrote that "the groundwork for this psy op (for lack of a better term) has been prepared for a long time."
Others, including researchers at Anthropic and OpenAI, have said Coxon's claims about the risk of AI wiping out humanity are well-founded.
"Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!" Evan Hubinger, the alignment science lead at Anthropic, wrote on X. "I personally think it is >10% within the next decade."
As for other perspectives that might be helpful, Delangue wrote in a reply that includes, "social scientists, other AI builders, futurists, investors, policymakers."
Delangue and Hugging Face's profiles have exploded since OpenAI announced in July that rogue AI models had broken containment during cybersecurity testing and breached Hugging Face in an effort to cheat on internal tests.
On September 3, Nvidia, which is highly reliant on AI-related demand for its chips, announced plans to acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. If policymakers were to slam the brakes on frontier AI development (a call some have renewed in the wake of Coxon's comments), Nvidia would likely be significantly affected.

title: Apple's new CEO was asked about 'pervert glasses.' Here was his response.
snippet:
Apple CEO John Ternus says the company wants "people around the user feel comfortable" about the Apple Watch's new AI listening features.
Carlos Barria/Reuters

Apple CEO John Ternus wants people to feel comfortable about the Apple Watch's new AI listening capabilities.
Ternus was asked about concerns about AI glasses, specifically that some have called them "pervert glasses."
Apple exec Greg Joswiak called it "quite a marketing slogan." Ternus stressed that the Apple Watch features don't record.

Apple would kindly like to stay far away from Meta's ongoing reputational challenges with AI glasses.
Apple CEO John Ternus was recently asked about how the company thinks about privacy in the age of AI wearables in light of backlash around AI glasses like Meta's. After all, Apple is rumored to be cooking up some AI glasses of its own in its labs.
"I know you can't talk about unannounced products, but what do you think about the backlash around what people are calling, you know, 'pervert glasses,'" Tom's Guide editor in chief Mark Spoonauer asked.

Before Ternus could answer, Greg Joswiak, Apple's senior vice president of worldwide marketing who also being interviewed, quipped: "That's quite a marketing slogan." The remark drew laughter from Ternus.
Meta is actively fighting back at that perception with a marketing blitz that emphasizes the AI glasses' light that alerts people when the recording feature is activated. It's also taken steps to thwart users who tamper with that light and pledged to remove "harassing" videos recorded by the AI glasses from Instagram (Business Insider has found those moderation efforts are off to a bumpy start.) Meta declined to comment on the Apple executives' remarks.
Beyond some laughter at a rival's expense, the pair of Apple execs instead looked to explain how the company hopes to address privacy concerns when it releases two new AI-enabled listening features alongside the next generation of Apple Watches.
"We wanted to do this in a way that people feel comfortable using it, and people around the user feel comfortable about its existence," Ternus said.
While its first foldable phone, iPhone Duo, stole the show, Apple also announced that Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 will come with optional "audio intelligence" features that, depending on a user's preference, can mean Siri is always listening to your conversations throughout the day. Apple says the features don't start working until the on-device AI detects speech and that no audio is recorded or stored.
Apple's Live Rewind Audio Intelligence feature on the new Apple Watch
Apple

One feature, "Siri Recap," can listen to meetings or even your whole day and generate what the company calls "high-level" notes on what happened. Another feature, Live Rewind, shows a text snippet of the last 15 seconds of what was just said around you on the Apple Watch's screen.
Ternus and Joswiak emphasized that neither feature includes speaker attribution. There's also no audio recording that the user could store for later playback. Apple also says it doesn't have access to the raw audio files. Joswiak also said this means Apple can't be compelled to turn over an audio file.
"It's just those higher-level notes to remind you of that without getting into all the stuff that really is privacy concerning which a lot of other products are doing," Joswiak said.
While they did not mention it, the Live Rewind feature also includes audio and visual cues on the Apple Watch's screen — similar to the recording light on Meta's AI glasses — to alert those around the watch wearer that the last 15 seconds of conversation is being processed. Apple says "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap" will be available in beta later this year.
Both Apple execs also said that current apps have long allowed users to record themselves and those around them. While they didn't mention anything in particular, AI-enabled apps and devices like Granola and Plaud are also designed for such use cases.
But the Apple execs' response to the question highlights that Apple is seeking to differentiate its approach to information-gathering on AI devices. Whether or not people ultimately feel comfortable about Apple Watches listening in on their conversations is another question altogether.

title: AI employees with apocalypse fears face a troubling question: Should they quit or stay?
snippet:
Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic
Bloomberg/Getty Images

Jacob Coxon's Anthropic exit sparked debate over whether to push for AI safety from inside or out.
The resignation also drew scrutiny over its impact on Anthropic's image and upcoming IPO.
AI workers' stay-or-go conundrum has a World War II parallel, a tech historian says.

AI workers with apocalypse fears are facing a troubling, though not unprecedented, career dilemma.
Should they quit their jobs to avoid potentially helping make the doomsday scenario they envision a reality? Or, should they drive change for the better from within?
It's a thorny predicament that came into focus this week when Jacob Coxon, a former OpenAI employee, said in an X post that he was resigning from Anthropic because the "people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade."
Soon after, Evan Hubinger, who leads Anthropic's alignment stress-testing team, essentially backed Coxon, saying he believes there is a greater-than-10% chance AI could kill all humans within the next decade.
Why some workers stay
For AI workers worried that they're contributing to mankind's destruction, deciding whether to quit or stay put is more complicated than it may seem, said Jeremie Harris, CEO and cofounder of Gladstone AI, a Washington, DC-based safety and advisory company focused on national security risks and catastrophic threats from advanced AI. "I don't particularly fault anyone for making either call," he said.
Harris said his job involves regularly talking with staff at Anthropic and other top AI labs, and that in recent months he's heard many express fears similar to those Coxon described. While quitting can be a moral response to building a dangerous technology, he said, Al labs could end up with few or no workers willing to press for change if resignations pile up.
"The people who are left are going to be the ones who are least concerned about safety," Harris said, while "people who care arguably should be the ones in the seat."
In response to Coxon's announcement, Anthropic employee Anna Wang said on X that she works at the company because she thinks she "can do better at reducing risks from the inside." She added that she respects and endorses others "who think that it's better to do so from the outside."
A spokesperson for Anthropic declined to comment after confirming Wang's employment.
Coxon's X post, which also sparked online debate over its impact on Anthropic's image, the company's coming IPO, and the possibility that this is all a strange publicity stunt, echoes concerns of a pending AI calamity previously made by Geoffrey Hinton, the computer scientist widely known as the "Godfather of AI," xAI founder Elon Musk, and others.
The general public is apprehensive about AI, too. Some 52% of Americans are more concerned than excited about the use of the technology in daily life, according to a June study from the Pew Research Center. That's up from 37% who said the same in 2021.
A dilemma with a history
For AI workers who truly believe their employer is creating an existential threat, Alex Wellerstein, a professor at Stevens Institute of Technology, said internal voices of reason have a poor track record of "overcoming preexisting institutional momentum."
"If you stick around, you're participating," he said.
That tension is not new. Technology historian Matthew H. Hersch said the Manhattan Project, a World War II-era program to develop nuclear weapons, is a close parallel.
Ralph Austin Bard, then undersecretary of the US Navy, privately urged officials to warn Japan before using the atomic bomb and resigned weeks before Hiroshima, likely in protest of the decision not to do so, said Hersch, also a professor at Harvard University and a member of the School of Historical Studies at the Institute for Advanced Study.
Other Manhattan Project scientists also unsuccessfully pushed for a demonstration of the bomb before it was used in combat, some of whom were effectively barred from future defense work, he added.
"Whistleblowers can do tremendous good," Hersch told Business Insider, "but are apt to be discredited or harassed into silence, and become unemployable in their industry."
